2.text: with a “Highest Chief of all the Chukchee,” as a kind of hereditary prince,

3.text: ruling the whole tribe. The family to whose lot this dignity fell was in reality

4.text: one of the richest reindeer-breeding families in the whole country. The head of

5.text: this family, in Maydell’s time, was Amraˊwkurg̣ɪn, a man of great personal

6.text: ability, both physical and moral. His father’s name was Yaˊtirg̣ɪn; and

7.text: Yaˊtirg̣ɪn’s father was Gêlaˊɪrg̣ɪn (“Marmot”). In a document of 1812 this

8.text: “Marmot” is called the “Chaun Chukchee Chief.” Khamakhei, in the document

9.text: of 1789 cited above, was also called “Chaun Chukchee Chief.” The western

10.text: limit of the Chukchee in that time lay near the Chaun River.

11.text: I mentioned before that the Russian authorities, from the very first years,

12.text: tried to find chiefs among the Chukchee, in order, through their mediation,

13.text: to exert an influence over the whole tribe. Since the Chukchee had no chiefs,

14.text: the Russian officials addressed their attentions simply to the more wealthy

15.text: and influential persons, and bribed them with presents, — gave them gaudy

16.text: coats, bright medals, and daggers inlaid with silver, — although usually with-

17.text: out practical result. Amraˊwkurg̣ɪn inherited from his father two such medals

18.text: and one coat. He was given several others besides; so that his son Eiˊheli

19.text: was able to hang form his neck, when in full parade dress, five ponderous

20.text: disks in yellow and white. Amraˊwkurg̣ɪn was very modest about displaying

21.text: his strange rank; but Eiˊheli, who had far less good sense than his father,

22.text: often presented quite a foolish appearance. I will quote the official report of

23.text: the chief official of the Kolyma for 1884: “This funny man came to me in

24.text: full parade, saying, ‘I am the Chukchee chief. I am the Czar.’”

25.text: I witnessed a meeting of Eiˊheli with another official newly come from

26.text: Yakutsk, and inexperienced in local affairs. Eiˊheli was quite drunk, and his

27.text: crimson coat was all besmeared with filth. Still, when he hiccoughed out his

28.text: usual “I am the Chukchee Czar,” the haughty official hastily stood up and

29.text: did obeisanse. After that, when Eiˊheli was going, he sped forwards and

30.text: opened the door with his own hand for the Chukchee majesty. Following

31.text: this example, the other Russians often called Eiˊheli “the black Chukchee

32.text: czar” or “the tundra czar.” I was witness to another occurrence, when a

33.text: well-to-do trader fell upon his knees before this dignitary with a complaint

34.text: against some Anui Chukchee who had charged too high a price for their

35.text: slaughtered reindeer. Eiˊheli said nothing: he had no influence with the people

36.text: in question. Other chiefs, supposed to rule their clans, have just as little

37.text: influence as the first dignitary. After a while, all the “clans” became mingled.

38.text: The supposed clansmen changed their abode, and quite forgot their former

39.text: relations. I remember that in the year 1895 one Toˊlɪño, an acquaintance of

40.text: mine, was made an assistant to the chief of the Anui clan. He told me very

41.text: judiciously, “Now I am a chief, and I have this dagger and a package of

42.text: papers as signs of my dignity. Still where in the world are my people?

43.text: I am unable to find any.”
